extracted.intended_audience: students, educators, and researchers interested in humour theory and verbal joke analysis (joke writers, linguists, teachers)
extracted.subtask_description: Apply the Script-Based Semantic Theory of Humour (SSTH) to analyze or craft verbal jokes by identifying script compatibility, script opposition/overlap, and punchline-triggered script shifts. Focused on linguistic/semantic frames that underlie written or spoken humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with two different (semantic) scripts
rubrics_metrics.description: The text is compatible, fully or in part, with two different (semantic) scripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raskin's first formal condition: for a verbal joke to work the same text must evoke at least two distinct scripts (semantic frames). Compatibility can be full or partial. Example: the whisper in the provided joke is compatible with both a 'Doctor' script and a 'Lover' script. When evaluating or creating jokes, verify that the wording plausibly evokes both scripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scripts must be opposite and overlapping
rubrics_metrics.description: The two scripts with which the text is compatible are opposite – the two scripts with which the text is compatible are said to overlap fully or in part on this text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raskin's second formal condition: the scripts must not merely be different but must stand in some form of opposition (e.g., Actual/Non-Actual, Normal/Abnormal). The overlap (full or partial) at the point of the text is crucial; check that the joke creates a locus where both opposed scripts can plausibly apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchline triggers abrupt script shift (primary → secondary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour is produced when there is a stimulus or trigger present at the end of the joke – commonly known as the punch-line. The punchline will cause the audience to abruptly shift their interpretation ... from the primary script (the more obvious script) to the secondary script (the alternative and less obvious script).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the punchline forces a rapid reinterpretation from the salient script to the alternative script. The timing and wording should make the primary script natural up to the punchline and then enable the sudden alternative interpretation (e.g., the wife's whispered 'Come right in' is nonsensical under the patient's Doctor script but sensible under a Lover script).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scripts are semantic frames/internalized cognitive structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripts include, for any given word, large chunks of semantic information surrounding the word and evoked by it and a cognitive structure internalised by the native speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or composing jokes, treat scripts as rich frames (beyond dictionary definitions) that include cultural knowledge, typical situations, and expectations. Recognize that native speakers have similar but not identical scripts; the joke must rely on sufficiently shared script elements to be understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: SSTH applies only to verbal humour (written and spoken)
rubrics_metrics.description: Due to its linguistic focus, SSTH only focuses on verbal humour. Verbal humour is considered as both written and spoken word, used in narrative, conversations, riddles and jokes where a humorous ending is present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SSTH principles when dealing with jokes, riddles, humorous narratives or conversational punchlines. Do not expect SSTH to directly model non-verbal humour (e.g., slapstick) unless that humour is linguistically mediated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script-opposition categories are finite and culturally dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: A partial list includes: Actual (Non-Actual); Normal (Abnormal); Possible (Impossible); Good (Bad); Life (Death); Obscene (Non-Obscene); Money (No-Money); High Stature (Low Stature. A complete list of possible scripts oppositions for jokes is finite and culturally dependent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying SSTH, consider which opposition category the joke exploits. Because the set of culturally salient oppositions is finite and varies by culture, evaluate jokes with attention to the audience's cultural background and which oppositions will be accessible or salient to them (e.g., Jewish humour vs Soviet political humour may use different oppositions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity plus overlap/association required (not mere juxtaposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although an incongruity is required to produce humour, the incongruities must overlap or be associated in some way. Without the connection between the two incongruities, or scripts in the case of this theory, humour will not be produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid creating jokes by simply putting two unrelated incongruous elements side by side. Effective verbal humour requires a clever connective element that allows the two scripts to 'make pseudo-sense together'—the reviewer/creator should check for an identifiable link or mechanism that enables the reinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary (salient) vs secondary (alternative) script dynamic
rubrics_metrics.description: One script functions as the primary (more obvious) script and the other as the secondary (alternative and less obvious) script; the punchline exploits the shift between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analysis or composition, ensure one reading is dominant throughout the setup (the primary script) so the punchline's reinterpretation toward the secondary script is surprising yet coherent. The clearer the initial salience and the more plausible the alternative, the stronger the effect.
